Comment Ownership: Visible but Forbidden

A genuine 403 case — the exception that shows the previous slide's 404 rule was a choice, not a blanket policy.

Editing or deleting a Comment breaks the previous slide's "hide it behind a 404" pattern on purpose, and the contrast is worth seeing directly:

// Figure 4.14: an ownership check that returns 403, not 404 (src/controllers/comment.controller.js, excerpt)
const assertCanModify = (comment, viewer) => {
  if (comment.authorId !== viewer.id && viewer.role !== 'admin') {
    throw new ApiError(403, 'You can only modify your own comments');
  }
};

By the time assertCanModify runs, findTicketOr404 and findCommentOr404 (Lesson 3's nested-resource pattern) have already succeeded — this viewer can already see both the ticket and this exact comment; GET .../comments/:id would return it to them right now. There's nothing left to hide: the comment's existence, its author, its body are all already visible to whoever's asking. What's actually being refused here is narrower — not "you can't see this," but "you can see this, and you may not change it, because you didn't write it." That's precisely what a 403 is for, and precisely why getTicketById's scoped 404 (previous slide) would be the wrong choice here — it would be hiding something this viewer can already see.

viewer.role !== 'admin' is the one exception: an admin can modify any comment, for moderation, regardless of who wrote it — a different axis of permission entirely from scopeForViewer's role-based ticket visibility, but the same underlying idea of "admin sees and can touch everything."
